source_review.notes: Reviewed the primary Herlihy-Wing, split-ordered-list, and hopscotch-hashing papers; current official Java SE 26 ConcurrentHashMap/ConcurrentMap, Go sync.Map, oneTBB concurrent_hash_map, and Python secure-hash documentation. All eight final destinations returned HTTP 200. Library claims are limited to their documented API contracts; paper performance is not generalized to current systems.

evidence: Checked key set K, values V, equivalence relation, partial map M, raw/spread hash, generation routing, load factor, migration states, history order, and measurement variables.
Checked bucket, stripe, generation, forwarding, tombstone, pin, live entry, logical deletion, physical retirement, and reclamation definitions.
Checked exact, approximate, weak, quiescent, per-key linearizable, and atomic-snapshot semantics remain distinct.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation connects the abstract one-mapping-per-equivalence-class contract to physical collision, migration, publication, and lifetime states.

evidence: Recomputed model routing for keys 0..9 from four old to eight new buckets, including keys 8 and 9 inserted on opposite sides of migration markers.
Recomputed ten mappings, square-value sum 285, four migrated old buckets, zero old entries, eight occupied new buckets, and mid-migration values 16 and 36.
Recomputed Exercise 2 modulo routing: old bucket 1 keys 1,5,9,13 route to new buckets 1 or 5.
numerical_recomputation.notes: No expected-time, collision, throughput, tail, or memory result is fabricated; the hypothetical benchmark value is explicitly rejected as sufficient evidence.

evidence: Verified equivalent keys require compatible hashes and at most one live abstract mapping independent of physical forwarding/copy state.
Verified locked migration ownership orders each old-bucket update either before transfer/inclusion or after marker/new routing, closing the lost-update gap.
Verified per-key linearizability does not compose into atomic two-key transfer or snapshot without a wider protocol.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The migration argument is conditional on monotonic authoritative state, coherent generation access, exclusive/idempotent transfer, target memory ordering, and delayed reclamation.

evidence: Reviewed empty/absence, duplicate equivalent keys, mutable keys, colliding bins, tombstones, hot keys, full capacity, allocation failure, and maximum growth.

Reviewed callback throw/block/reentry/replay, same-key conditional races, migration abandoned mid-bucket, lookup during handoff, duplicate physical copies, deletion/ABA, clear/close, and stale generations.
Reviewed weak iteration, exact count versus snapshot, bulk operations, tenant exhaustion, chosen collision attacks, expensive equality/values, authorization cache staleness, and diagnostics.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Resource requirements cover entries/bytes, collision/probe/help work, callback duration, retry/wait, retained generations, per-tenant budgets, and expiry/cleanup.

evidence: The finite model routes by a monotonic per-old-bucket marker, migrates idempotently, clears transferred old buckets, and combines old/new snapshots without key loss.
Exact assertions cover key set 0..9, sum 285, all markers, zero old entries, and two successful mid-resize observations.
Chapter invariants cover hash/equivalence, unique live mapping, reachability, initialization/visibility, conditional atomicity, resize, guarding, callbacks, aggregates, and resource limits.
invariant_checking.notes: Model methods are indivisible by construction and therefore do not instantiate the lock/atomic handoff a production concurrent implementation requires.

evidence: Reviewed map-operation proof from generation pin and routing through protected predicate, publication, linearization, invariant restoration, retirement, and cleanup.
Reviewed resize obligations for construction, authoritative bucket state, update/transfer ordering, false absence, conditional operations, uniqueness, count, helper failure, and reclamation.
Reviewed separate-chaining, open-addressing, hopscotch, cuckoo, split-order, striped, sharded, persistent, actor, and nonblocking trade-offs without transferring guarantees.
proof_review.notes: No unspecified library or custom implementation is declared correct; each architecture must instantiate memory ordering, progress, collision, resize, and reclamation details.

evidence: The central migration claim is explicitly a conditional proof pattern rather than validation of arbitrary dual-table search.
The bounded program is labeled a deterministic state model without thread, lock, failure, memory-order, arbitrary-hash, or schedule coverage.
Expected O(1), library API semantics, paper algorithms, security defenses, and performance measurements are scoped to named assumptions/sources.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No race-detector, benchmark, final-state, or per-key result is allowed to imply whole-map transactions, snapshot atomicity, liveness, or deployment fitness.

evidence: The standard-library-only finite Python resize model passed exact ten-line stdout, empty stderr, and zero exit status under the repository verifier.
It emits evidence=finite_incremental_resize_model and reproduces old/new routing, inserts before/after migration, complete transfer, and exact final-state assertions.
All eight external destinations returned HTTP 200 and repository-local links passed chapter validation.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No runtime concurrency, locks/atomics, memory visibility, arbitrary histories, collision/fault/cancellation, ABA/reclamation, sanitizer/lockdep, capacity attack, or performance experiment was run.

conceptual_review.notes: The chapter starts from an abstract concurrent-map contract, derives collision/publication/linearization rules, treats resize as an ownership transition, and separates per-key operations from aggregates, callbacks, lifetime, security, progress, and performance.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed API selection across Java, Go, and oneTBB; stable keys; conditional methods; callback scope; publication; old/new migration handoff; exact count and weak views; deletion/reclamation; capacity/tenant defense; diagnostics; correctness tooling; workload metrics; and rollback criteria.

pedagogical_review.notes: The review sheet supports retrieval; the finite model isolates migration ownership; ten examples cover composition, attacks, mutable keys, lost updates, counts, callbacks, views, ABA, accessor lifetime, and benchmarking; five progressive exercises have complete model answers.

limitations: Internal authoring, primary/official-source, mathematical, bounded executable-model, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical evidence only; no external academic, Herlihy/Wing, Shalev/Shavit, Herlihy/Shavit/Tzafrir, Oracle, Go, oneTBB, Python, security, performance, reliability, or independent practitioner review is claimed. The chapter and finite model prove neither a concrete concurrent map, runtime threads/locks/atomics, target memory visibility, arbitrary histories/interleavings/hashes/callbacks, collision bounds, progress/fairness, crash/cancellation recovery, ABA/reclamation safety, exact aggregate snapshots, hash-flood resistance, tenant isolation, production latency/throughput/cache/NUMA behavior, certification, nor deployment fitness.
